title: The obstacle becomes the way
hookLine: what stands in the way of action advances action (Meditations 5.20)

cards: The flight is canceled. The coworker you need is out sick. The kid spills juice on the one clean shirt five minutes before you leave.
You had a plan, and now there's a thing in the road. Most of us treat that thing as the end of the day's story: well, that ruined it.
Marcus had a whole empire of things in the road: plague, war on the northern border, a trusted general who revolted against him, a court full of difficult people.
And in Book Five he wrote himself a note that became one of the most quoted lines in all of Stoic writing.

teach.b: What's surprising is who Marcus was talking about: people. Other people are the closest thing to him, he says, because his job is to do them good and put up with them.
But when someone blocks what he's trying to do, that person becomes, for the moment, like the sun, or the wind, or a wild animal: something in the way of his action. Then comes the turn.
They can block what he does, but not his intention or his attitude, because the mind can adapt. It can turn a hindrance into help.
What stood in the way of acting becomes a way of acting, and what blocks the road moves you along it. How does that work? The Stoics had an idea sometimes called the reserve clause.
You set out to do something, adding quietly: if nothing prevents it. If something does, you haven't failed. You've been handed a new task: to meet this well.
The canceled flight becomes a lesson in patience. The rude coworker becomes practice in fairness. The spilled juice becomes a chance to be kind to a kid who already feels terrible.
A popular modern book on Stoicism takes its title from this passage, The Obstacle Is the Way.
Marcus's own words are gentler and more precise: an obstacle can't stop the part of you that chooses how to respond, so it can always become the next step.

how: Many readers of the Stoics practice the reserve clause, planning with the silent addition 'if nothing prevents it', and treat setbacks as the next task rather than the end of the plan.

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus wrote 'the obstacle is the way' in those exact words
that's the title of a modern book. Marcus says the obstacle on the road helps you along it.
the passage begins with people getting in the way
he says others can block his action, like the wind or a wild animal.
Marcus says an obstacle can block your intention
it can block what you do, but not your intention or how you respond.

games.q: you're Marcus. someone at court is blocking what you're trying to do. what do you tell yourself?
o: they have ruined my plan; nothing can be done.
they can block my action, not my intention; this becomes my next task.
remove everyone who ever gets in my way.
games.why: Marcus says the mind turns every hindrance into help, so what blocks the road moves you along it.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your way right now, a person, a delay, a problem, a limit, and look at it without arguing with it. Then ask quietly: what could this make possible?
Patience, a better plan, a kinder word; one small new step is enough.

wordCard.voice: Reserve clause. The Stoics' habit of adding 'if nothing prevents it' to a plan, so what blocks your action becomes the way you act instead. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: a hindrance, literally something at your feet. the word for what gets in the way.

carryVoice: Your line: the way through. If something blocks the plan, meeting it well is the next task. Day one hundred ninety-seven, done.
